lead: Avionics electronics is the layer between the transducers and the computers. A bridge gives a few millivolts; an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) wants volts in a clean, limited band; a microcontroller turns the numbers into decisions; and a transistor or a digital-to-analog converter (DAC) drives the actuator. The same chain sits inside an air data computer, a fuel-quantity unit and a flap controller.
prereq: You need: Aircraft transducers for the bridge output used here.

blocks.text: A diode conducts from anode to cathode once the forward voltage is about 0.7 V (silicon) and blocks the other way. In aircraft it is used as a rectifier (transformer rectifier units turn 115 V AC into 28 V DC), as a flyback diode across a relay or solenoid coil, and as a Zener or transient-voltage suppressor that clamps spikes from switching and lightning.

A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) has base, collector and emitter. In the active region it amplifies: IC = β IB, where β is the current gain. As a switch it is driven into saturation with more base current than IC ÷ β, so VCE falls to about 0.2 V and little power is lost. A MOSFET is switched by its gate voltage and draws almost no gate current; power MOSFETs switch pumps, lights and motors, and are the switches inside solid-state power controllers.

An operational amplifier is a very high-gain differential amplifier. With negative feedback two rules solve most circuits: no current flows into the inputs, and the output makes the two input voltages equal.
Inverting: A = −R<sub>f</sub> ÷ R<sub>in</sub>     Non-inverting: A = 1 + R<sub>f</sub> ÷ R<sub>in</sub>
blocks.where: A is the voltage gain; Rf is the feedback resistor from the output to the inverting input; Rin goes from the inverting input to the signal (inverting) or to ground (non-inverting). A voltage follower (output tied to the inverting input, no resistors) has A = 1, very high input resistance and low output resistance.

blocks.text: A differential amplifier uses one op-amp and four resistors; with R₁ = R₃ and R₂ = R₄ it amplifies the difference of its inputs by R₂ ÷ R₁ and rejects the voltage common to both. A bridge output is a small difference riding on half the excitation. The instrumentation amplifier does this with three op-amps: two input followers with gain and a difference stage. Its gain is G = 1 + 2R ÷ RG, set by one resistor RG.

Signal conditioning then means: amplify to fill the ADC range; filter (an anti-alias low-pass filter removes noise above half the sampling rate; a first-order RC filter has cut-off fc = 1 ÷ (2πRC)); isolate where grounds differ; clamp the inputs; and linearise in software.
Q = V<sub>ref</sub> ÷ 2<sup>N</sup>     code = floor(V<sub>in</sub> ÷ Q), at most 2<sup>N</sup> − 1
blocks.where: Q is the resolution (one step) in volts; V<sub>ref</sub> is the reference voltage; N is the number of bits; V<sub>in</sub> is the input; floor rounds down. With this rounding-down rule the quantisation error is between 0 and one step; a converter that rounds to the nearest step has an error of at most ±Q ÷ 2.

blocks.text: Converter types: successive approximation (SAR), the usual general-purpose type, tries one bit at a time from the most significant, so an N-bit conversion takes N steps; flash uses 2N − 1 comparators for the fastest conversion; sigma-delta oversamples and filters to give 16 to 24 bits for slow signals such as pressure and temperature; dual-slope suits meters. The sampling rate must be more than twice the highest frequency present (the Nyquist rule), or higher frequencies fold back as false low ones (aliasing).
A DAC does the reverse: Vout = k × Vref ÷ 2N for code k. A DAC output needs a buffer or power amplifier to drive a servo valve coil.

A microprocessor is a CPU on a chip; memory and input/output are separate chips. A microcontroller puts the CPU, flash program memory, RAM, timers, an ADC, digital input/output and serial ports (UART, SPI, I²C, CAN) on one chip, so a sensor or actuator controller needs few other parts. A typical loop runs at a fixed rate: read the ADC, filter and scale, check limits, update the outputs, send the value on the bus and kick the watchdog timer, which resets the chip if the loop ever stops.

examples.question: The pressure transducer of the previous chapter gives 0 to 20 mV for 0 to 100 kPa. An instrumentation amplifier with R = 25 kΩ feeds a 12-bit ADC with V<sub>ref</sub> = 4.096 V. (a) Find R<sub>G</sub> for a gain of 200. (b) R<sub>G</sub> is fitted as the standard 249 Ω. Find the real gain and the full-scale amplifier output. (c) Find the ADC resolution and the code at 35 kPa. (d) Find the pressure represented by one code.
steps: With 249 Ω: G = 1 + 50 000 ÷ 249 = 201.8. Full scale: 20 mV × 201.8 = 4.036 V, below 4.096 V, so the ADC never clips.
At 35 kPa the bridge gives 7.0 mV (0.20 mV/kPa). Amplifier output: 7.0 mV × 201.8 = 1.4126 V. Code = floor(1.4126 ÷ 0.001) = 1412.
Full scale is 4.036 V ÷ 1 mV = 4036 codes for 100 kPa, so one code is 100 ÷ 4036 = 0.0248 kPa (about 25 Pa).
examples.answer: R<sub>G</sub> = 251.3 Ω ideal; with 249 Ω the gain is 201.8 and full scale is 4.036 V; Q = 1 mV; 35 kPa gives code 1412; one code is about 0.025 kPa.

examples.question: A microcontroller with a 5 V output pin switches a 28 V solenoid of resistance 70 Ω and inductance 0.1 H through an NPN transistor with β ≥ 100. (a) Find the coil current. (b) Choose the base resistor for a base current twice the minimum. (c) What voltage would appear if the current fell to zero in 1 µs with no flyback diode?
steps: Coil current: I<sub>C</sub> = 28 V ÷ 70 Ω = 0.40 A (ignoring the 0.2 V saturation drop).
Minimum base current: 0.40 ÷ 100 = 4 mA. With a factor of 2 for hard saturation: I<sub>B</sub> = 8 mA.
Base resistor: R<sub>B</sub> = (5 − 0.7) ÷ 0.008 = 537.5 Ω; the next lower standard value, 510 Ω, gives (5 − 0.7) ÷ 510 = 8.4 mA. The pin must be able to source 8.4 mA.

Without a diode: V = L di/dt = 0.1 × 0.40 ÷ (1 × 10⁻⁶) = 40 000 V in theory. The transistor breaks down long before that, so a flyback diode across the coil (cathode to +28 V) is fitted; it carries the 0.40 A as the field collapses.
examples.answer: I<sub>C</sub> = 0.40 A; R<sub>B</sub> = 510 Ω (8.4 mA); without a flyback diode the switch-off spike would reach tens of kilovolts in theory and destroy the transistor.

traps: Writing Q = V<sub>ref</sub> ÷ 2N. It is V<sub>ref</sub> divided by 2 to the power N: 5 V ÷ 2⁸ = 19.5 mV.
Using A = R<sub>f</sub> ÷ R<sub>in</sub> for a non-inverting amplifier. It is 1 + R<sub>f</sub> ÷ R<sub>in</sub>.
Fitting the flyback diode the wrong way round. Cathode to the positive supply; reversed, it shorts the supply whenever the coil is on.
Giving a BJT switch exactly I<sub>C</sub> ÷ β of base current. It sits in the active region and overheats; drive it into saturation.

quiz.q: Name four blocks on a microcontroller chip that a microprocessor lacks.
quiz.a: Flash program memory, RAM, timers, ADC, digital input/output, serial ports (any four).

quiz.q: Why is an instrumentation amplifier used for a bridge instead of a simple inverting amplifier?
quiz.a: Its inputs draw almost no current, so they do not load the bridge, and it amplifies only the difference while rejecting the large common-mode voltage.

quiz.q: A 10-bit ADC has V<sub>ref</sub> = 4.096 V. Find Q and the code for 1.000 V.
An 8-bit DAC with V<sub>ref</sub> = 5 V receives code 200. Find the output.
A non-inverting amplifier has R<sub>f</sub> = 9 kΩ and R<sub>in</sub> = 1 kΩ. Find the output for 0.2 V in, and the error if R<sub>f</sub> drifts to 10 kΩ.
quiz.a: A = 1 + 9 = 10, output 2.0 V. With 10 kΩ, A = 11 and output 2.2 V: a 10 % error, which is why precision resistors are used.

quiz.q: Why does a sensor microcontroller have a watchdog timer?
quiz.a: If the software hangs, the loop stops kicking the watchdog and it resets the chip, so the sensor recovers instead of sending a frozen value.

beyond: Not for the exam. Sigma-delta converters with digital filters have replaced most analog filtering in slow sensor channels. Search for 'instrumentation amplifier CMRR', 'SAR ADC', 'solid-state power controller' and 'DO-254'.

figure.caption: The two worked examples as one chain. Top: 35 kPa gives 7.0 mV at the bridge, 1.4126 V after the gain of 201.8 and code 1412 from the 12-bit ADC. Bottom: the microcontroller pin drives the transistor through 510 Ω, the transistor switches 0.40 A through the solenoid, and the flyback diode absorbs the switch-off spike.

spec.aria: Top row of blocks: bridge, instrumentation amplifier with gain 201.8, anti-alias filter, 12-bit ADC with 1 millivolt steps, microcontroller. Values under them: 7.0 millivolts, 1.4126 volts, 1.4126 volts, code 1412, 35.0 kilopascals. Bottom row, from right to left: a 5 volt pin with a 510 ohm base resistor giving 8.4 milliamps, an NPN transistor switch, a 70 ohm 0.1 henry solenoid carrying 0.40 amps, and a flyback diode across the coil; without it the spike would be 40 kilovolts.
